newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Prospects for Portugal bound by EMU.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Prospects for Portugal bound by EMU.

text.p: Portuguese bonds have value to offer investors over the coming months but may waver depending on bond market sentiment towards European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), analysts said on Tuesday.
Fundamental targets are on track for Portugal to meet criteria needed to join EMU at the start, but some doubt whether Portugal would join if Spain failed to qualify.
"Spain is one of those markets vulnerable to a change in foreign investors' perceptions over EMU," said Ken Wattret, economist at Paribas in London.
"And in the short term the Portuguese market will continue to be driven by what happens in Spain."
He said while European bond markets were going up and optimism over EMU remained buoyant, the yield spread between Portuguese and Spanish bonds would widen and the Portugal/Germany gap would narrow.
"But in the current climate we are seeing more concerns about EMU participation and about whether convergence at these levels is sustainable," Wattret said.

"Given that Portugal has liquidity problems relative to Spain, it points to the two markets trading closely together and the bias in the short term being to spread widening over Germany rather than narrowing."
The 10-year Portuguese/German yield spread was last at 106 basis points, having widened from 89 at the end of January. The Spanish/German gap had also widened to 116 basis points from 94.
Juli Collins-Thompson, economist at Yamaichi International in London, was optimistic for Portugal and Spain over the coming months and saw possibilities for further convergence.
Both were likely to be included in the first round of EMU, she said.
"There is still a substantial risk premium built into the market and we are expecting spreads to continue to narrow. We are officially projecting 40 basis points within a year's time," she said.
"As the year goes on we'll see growing confidence for both Spain and Portugal."

Wattret said in terms of fundamentals Portugal looked favourable relative to both Spain and Italy. "Because the fiscal convergence so far has been more pronounced, Portugal begins this year with a lower budget deficit and relatively healthy political stability and a broad public commitment towards monetary union," he said.

The sustained economic progress and policies of financial stability were reflected on Monday by Moody's Investors Service raising its sovereign ceiling for Portual's foreign currency debt and bank deposits to Aa3 from A1.
But when it came to the crunch, he was uncertain that Portugal would go into EMU if Spain failed to make the grade.

Collins-Thompson said the argument for Portugal not going into EMU without Spain was a fair one, given their heavy interdependence for trade, but she said Yamaichi forecasts were for both to qulaify, thus eliminating the problem.

Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW in London, thought it unlikely Portugal would go into EMU without Spain even if it met the criteria, and saw little further convergence for Portuguese bonds for now.

"You have to remember to factor in an EMU breakup premium, particularly if Portugal, Spain and Italy were all in the first round," she said. "We are not guaranteed the whole thing is going to hold together."
"You have to add back some yield and for Spain, Portugal and Italy . Those spreads are going to be pretty high, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 100 basis points."
Reed said a credit spread of around 20 to 30 basis points for Portugal, and the possibility that EMU may not happen at all, also needed to be included.
"You add all that together and you wonder if there is really a lot of value in Portugal at the moment," she said.
